questions.q: What is the main inefficiency of classic request-level dynamic batching for LLM workloads?
options: It cannot run on GPUs at all
A batch runs as a fixed unit until every request in it finishes, so a request that finishes early leaves its GPU slot idle until the whole batch ends
It requires every request to have exactly the same prompt
It uses more GPU memory than static batching in every case
questions.explain: Because LLM requests generate different numbers of output tokens, they finish at different times, but request-level batching can't admit a new request into a slot freed early — that slot sits idle until the entire batch completes.

questions.q: What does continuous (iteration-level) batching change about scheduling?
options: It schedules requests once per day instead of per batch
It makes scheduling decisions after every single decode step, admitting new requests into freed slots immediately
It removes the need for a KV cache entirely
It only works for requests with identical prompt lengths
questions.explain: Continuous batching checks after every decode step which requests finished and immediately fills their slots with new requests, so batch composition can change every iteration rather than only between whole batches.

questions.q: Why does continuous batching depend on PagedAttention's block-based memory model?
options: It doesn't — the two techniques are unrelated

Swapping requests in and out of the batch every step requires allocating and freeing cache memory constantly, which only works efficiently with flexible, block-by-block allocation rather than large contiguous reservations
PagedAttention eliminates the need for scheduling altogether
Continuous batching only applies to prefill, which doesn't use the KV cache
questions.explain: Without PagedAttention's ability to allocate cache memory in small blocks on demand, swapping requests in and out of the running batch every single step would require expensive, constant memory reshuffling.

questions.q: What problem does chunked prefill solve?
options: It prevents any new requests from joining a running batch
A new request's compute-heavy prefill step can stall the decode steps of requests already running, so prefill is split into smaller chunks interleaved with ongoing decode
It removes the need for continuous batching entirely
It only affects requests that have already finished generating
questions.explain: Chunked prefill splits a long prompt's prefill into smaller pieces that fit alongside ongoing decode steps in the same iteration, instead of forcing one large prefill to run in exclusive isolation and stall other requests.

questions.q: In continuous batching, how does one request's lifetime relate to another's within the running batch?
options: Every request must start and finish at exactly the same time
A request's lifetime is independent — it joins when there's room and leaves the moment it's done, regardless of other requests
Only one request can be processed at a time
Requests are processed strictly in the order they were submitted, with no overlap
questions.explain: Continuous batching breaks the 'whole batch moves together' assumption — each request joins the batch when a slot is free and leaves as soon as it finishes, independent of any other request's progress.
